title: Silas and the Silence
premise: After her mother's funeral, August Oyelaran returns to the family house in Lagos to sort a lifetime of unspoken things, only to be approached by a stranger who calls her family by a name no one has used since before she was born. Following her mother's letters, a locked room, and her father's evasions, August uncovers the identity her parents buried to survive a political purge decades ago. As the last witness to that night is dying, August must decide whether recovering the truth will free her or cost her the fragile family that silence built. In the end, she speaks the name aloud at her mother's grave, choosing memory over safety, and inherits not the secret but the courage it took to keep it.
about_author: Ivo Eriksen is the pen name of a Nigerian-Danish writer raised between Lagos and Aarhus, whose work examines inheritance, exile, and the grammar of things left unsaid. Silas and the Silence is their second novel, written over seven years in rented rooms on two continents.

chapters.title: The House That Held Its Breath
chapters.summary: August's POV. Days after the funeral, August catalogues her mother's belongings with archival precision, avoiding the locked study. The emotional beat is controlled grief masking dread; she has returned home but behaves like a stranger in it.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: August's POV. At the wake's end, an elderly stranger grips her hand and says, 'Tell Silas I saw him.' August realizes he means her father, and that 'Silas' is not his name. Beat: the first crack in twenty years of practiced ignorance.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: August's POV, with flashbacks. She rehearses asking her father and fails at dinner, as she has failed for two decades. Her brother Tunde deflects with jokes. Beat: the family choreography of avoidance performed one more time.

chapters.title: The Locked Study
chapters.summary: August's POV. She finds her mother's key hidden in a hymnal and opens the study: boxes of letters addressed to a woman named Adaeze, all unanswered. Beat: grief curdles into suspicion; the archive of silence is real.

chapters.title: Letters to Adaeze
chapters.summary: August's POV. Reading the earliest letters, dated 1979, she learns her mother wrote yearly to someone she called sister. The handwriting grows shakier, more desperate. Beat: August understands her mother was also a keeper of someone else's secret.

chapters.title: Silas
chapters.summary: Father's POV, 1981. A young man named Chidi takes a new name, new papers, and a new city after a night of soldiers and fire. Beat: terror rendered in flat bureaucratic language; survival begins with erasure.

chapters.title: What Tunde Knows
chapters.summary: Tunde's POV. Confronted gently by August, Tunde admits he learned fragments years ago and chose not to know more. Beat: sibling rupture and tenderness; two children of silence comparing wounds.

chapters.title: The Stranger Returns
chapters.summary: August's POV. The old man, Mr. Okonkwo, waits outside the house. He was there the night Chidi became Silas; he says the last other witness, Mama Ngozi, is dying in Enugu. Beat: urgency enters the story; time becomes an antagonist.

chapters.title: My Mother's Handwriting
chapters.summary: August's POV. Among the letters she finds her mother's unsent final draft, confessing what happened and begging forgiveness. It stops mid-sentence. Beat: devastation; the confession August needed died unfinished.

chapters.title: Road to Enugu
chapters.summary: August's POV. Against her father's plea, she travels east with Tunde. Landscapes and memories blur; she interviews her own childhood en route. Beat: departure as transformation; the daughter leaves the house of silence.

chapters.title: Mama Ngozi
chapters.summary: August's POV. The dying woman receives them, lucid in intervals, and calls August by Adaeze's resemblance. She promises the whole story if they return tomorrow. Beat: hope shadowed by mortality; the truth has a heartbeat now.

chapters.title: The Night of the Fire
chapters.summary: Mama Ngozi's POV, 1981. The purge reaches the compound: names read aloud, neighbors taken, a fire set to destroy records—and people. Chidi escaped because Adaeze stayed behind. Beat: horror told with terrible calm.

chapters.title: Adaeze
chapters.summary: Mama Ngozi's POV. Adaeze, August's aunt, drew the soldiers away so her brother could flee, and was never seen again. The name 'Oyelaran' was bought, the past buried. Beat: revelation of the central sacrifice; grief reorganized around a ghost.

chapters.title: Father, Unmasked
chapters.summary: August's POV. She calls her father from Enugu and says 'Chidi' aloud. Long silence, then weeping—the first she has ever heard from him. Beat: the question finally asked; the family's architecture cracks open.

chapters.title: He Comes East
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Silas arrives in Enugu, aged and diminished, and sits with Mama Ngozi. They speak in the old language of before. Beat: reconciliation without absolution; two survivors holding the same night.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, present day. He tells August why he stayed silent: witness protection ended long ago, but shame outlived danger. Every year of silence made speaking more impossible. Beat: compassion replaces anger; August sees her own almost-sayings mirrored.

chapters.title: The Funeral Within the Funeral
chapters.summary: August's POV. Mama Ngozi dies peacefully. At her burial, Silas publicly speaks Chidi's name and Adaeze's for the first time in forty years. Beat: catharsis; mourning doubles as resurrection.

chapters.title: Searching for Adaeze
chapters.summary: August and Tunde's POV. Following records, they find Adaeze survived, fled to Accra, lived under another name, and died in 2011—leaving a daughter. Beat: bittersweet discovery; the lost aunt left a living thread.

chapters.title: Cousins
chapters.summary: August's POV. In Accra, August meets Efua, Adaeze's daughter, who grew up with her own version of silence. Two inheritances meet. Beat: cautious kinship; the secret's cost revealed across generations.

chapters.title: The Archive of Speaking
chapters.summary: August's POV. Back home, August reverses her catalogue: instead of boxing the past away, she builds an archive—letters, testimonies, photographs—to be shared with the whole family. Beat: agency reclaimed; memory curated rather than buried.

chapters.title: Silas and the Silence
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Father and daughter sit in the unlocked study. He gives her the last piece: a letter Adaeze smuggled out, which he could never bear to open. Together they read it. Beat: intimacy earned through truth; the title resolves.

chapters.title: August
chapters.summary: August's POV. At her mother's grave, August speaks every name aloud—Adaeze, Chidi, her mother's own buried middle name—and reads the finished confession she has written to complete her mother's unfinished sentence. Beat: resolution; she inherits not the secret but the voice, and the family gathers around a table where nothing needs hiding.
